questions.lessonTitle: Octavian's Ascension and Title of Augustus
questions.lessonContent: Octavian was sole ruler of Rome after his forces defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium. The Senate gave him the name "Augustus," meaning "most high." In 23 BCE, Octavian, now referred to as Augustus, was made consul for life by the Senate. He was also made "Princeps," meaning "first citizen," which is the origin of the word "prince." He was further given the title "Imperator," meaning "successful general," which is the origin of the word "emperor.
questions.question: What title meaning "most high" was given to Octavian by the Senate?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Rome controlled the entire Mediterranean region and beyond, achieving complete control that meant almost no warfare. This peace lasted nearly 200 years. During this period, more and more provincials were granted official Roman citizenship. The Pax Romana represented a time of unprecedented stability and prosperity across the Roman world.
questions.question: The Pax Romana was a period of peace that lasted nearly 200 years.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: Early Roman Emperors and Hereditary Succession
questions.lessonContent: After Augustus, there was great variety in the quality of emperors who succeeded him. The office of emperor was initially designed to be hereditary, but from the start, there was confusion as to which family member would inherit the throne. Some emperors proved to be cutthroats, or insane, or both. The military came to play an enormous role in selecting who would become emperor. Caligula exiled, killed, or forced suicide on members of his own family and perceived enemies before being assassinated in 41 CE by members of the Praetorian Guard. Nero murdered his mother, his stepbrother, two of his wives, and his teacher Seneca, and was forced to commit suicide.
questions.question: Which early emperor was the son of famed military leader Germanicus and earned his nickname "Caligula" (meaning "little boots") from the Roman army as a child?
questions.explanation: Caligula was the son of Germanicus, the nephew and adopted son of Tiberius. He earned his name "Caligula" meaning "little boots" by the Roman army as a child because he was dressed like a soldier.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: Module 1: The Rise and Establishment of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: After Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, the Senate gave him the name 'Augustus,' meaning 'most high.' Then, in 23 BCE, Octavian (now referred to as Augustus) was made consul for life by the Senate. These three events show how Octavian transitioned from military victor to Rome's first emperor.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Octavian's rise to become Augustus?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Transformation, Division, and Fall of the Empire
questions.lessonTitle: Diocletian's Administrative Division of the Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian believed that dividing the empire for administrative purposes would strengthen it. In 285 CE, he divided the empire into two administrative realms: the Eastern (Byzantine) Empire and the Western (Roman) Empire. This was the first step in the creation of what would become two separate empires. Diocletian also increased the bureaucracy for more effective administration and was the first emperor in 100 years to properly restore order after the Crisis of the Third Century.
questions.question: Who divided the Roman Empire into Eastern and Western administrative realms, and in what year?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Transformation, Division, and Fall of the Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Constantine's mother, Helena, had converted to Christianity before him. The Edict of Milan in 313 CE legalized Christianity and established religious toleration throughout the empire. However, Constantine only converted to Christianity on his deathbed, not at the beginning or during the height of his reign. Despite his delayed conversion, Constantine's endorsement of Christianity fundamentally changed the religion's status in the Roman Empire.
questions.question: Constantine converted to Christianity at the beginning of his reign to gain Christian support.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Transformation, Division, and Fall of the Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Official End of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer. This event marks the traditional date used by historians to pinpoint the fall of the Western Roman Empire. The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire continued to exist until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. The east/west split had deepened significantly once Constantine set up Constantinople as the new capital city.
questions.question: When did the Western Roman Empire officially end?
questions.explanation: The Western Roman Empire officially ended in 476 CE when the last emperor Romulus Augustus was deposed by the barbarian Odoacer. This is the traditional date historians use for the fall of the Western Roman Empire.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Transformation, Division, and Fall of the Empire
questions.lessonTitle: The Year of the Four Emperors
questions.lessonContent: The Year of the Four Emperors (69 CE) was a brief period of civil war after the death of Emperor Nero. The succession crisis began when Nero died in 68 CE, leading to Galba becoming emperor. Otho then overthrows Galba, but Vitellius defeats Otho in battle. Finally, Vespasian defeats Vitellius and establishes a new stable dynasty. This chaotic year illustrates the problems of imperial succession in the early Roman Empire.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Year of the Four Emperors succession crisis?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Lasting Contributions of Roman Civilization
questions.lessonTitle: The Justinian Code and Roman Law
questions.lessonContent: Roman law began with the Twelve Tables in 450 BCE and developed over a thousand years, including decisions of judges, ideas of the Republic and Empire, and rulings of emperors. It encompassed public law (relationship of citizen to state), private or civil law (relationships between people), and jus gentium (rights of foreigners). Emperor Justinian rewrote Roman law in the 6th century CE, creating the Corpus Juris Civilis, also known as the Justinian Code. This code encapsulated the previous thousand years of Roman law development and still serves as the basis for civil law in several European countries today.
questions.question: What did Emperor Justinian create that encapsulated over 1000 years of Roman law and still serves as the basis for civil law in several countries today?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Lasting Contributions of Roman Civilization
questions.lessonContent: The term 'Romance' meaning 'Roman' refers to languages that developed from Latin. These include French, Italian, Portuguese, Romanian, and Spanish. Old English was a Germanic language, but when William the Conqueror from Normandy brought French to England in 1066, Middle English emerged as a mixture of these old Germanic and French languages. Today, approximately half of modern English can be traced to Latin. Additionally, Latin has traditionally been used as a universal language in science, with our scientific names and most legal and medical terminology being Latin-based.
questions.question: True or false: Romance languages developed from Latin.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Lasting Contributions of Roman Civilization
questions.lessonContent: A large part of Rome's success was due to the importance Rome placed on building and maintaining the empire's infrastructure, including aqueducts, bridges, dams, harbors, and roads. Public buildings included amphitheaters like the Colosseum, basilicas, government offices, palaces, public baths, and theaters. While the Romans copied their basic architectural style from the Greeks, they adapted the arch from the Etruscans and put it to great use in construction such as aqueducts. The Romans also developed the dome and vault architectural techniques.
questions.question: Which architectural element did the Romans adapt from the Etruscans and use in the construction of aqueducts?
questions.explanation: The Romans adapted the arch from the Etruscans and effectively used it in constructing aqueducts, bridges, and other significant infrastructure projects.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: Lasting Contributions of Roman Civilization
questions.lessonContent: Roman law began with the Twelve Tables in 450 BCE, which created a written code of laws for Rome. Throughout the Republic Era, additional laws were added by the Senate and assembly. During the Empire period, rulings by emperors became another source of law. Judicial decisions by judges also contributed to the legal system. Finally, Emperor Justinian compiled all these sources of law into a comprehensive code in the 6th century CE.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the development of Roman law?

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent research system consists of multiple agents, which are LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish complex tasks. The system uses an orchestrator-worker pattern where a lead agent coordinates the research process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. Each subagent acts as an intelligent filter by iteratively using search tools to gather information before returning findings to the lead agent for synthesis. The architecture enables the system to handle research tasks that exceed the capacity of single agents.
questions.question: What is the architectural pattern used in the Research system described?

questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent research systems achieve high performance primarily by scaling token usage to solve complex problems. In the BrowseComp evaluation, which tests the ability of browsing agents to locate hard-to-find information, token usage alone explains 80% of the performance variance. The number of tool calls and model choice are the two other explanatory factors that together account for the remaining 15% of variance. Multi-agent architectures distribute work across agents with separate context windows, adding capacity for parallel reasoning. This allows the system to process information that exceeds single context windows and accomplish tasks that would be impossible for individual agents.
questions.question: Token usage explains 80% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation.

questions.lessonContent: Internal evaluations at Anthropic demonstrated that multi-agent research systems significantly outperform single-agent approaches for breadth-first queries. A multi-agent system using Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on their internal research evaluation. This test involved identifying all board members of companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, where the multi-agent system succeeded by decomposing the task into parallel subtasks for subagents while the single agent system failed with slow, sequential searches. The performance gain validates that multi-agent systems excel at tasks requiring exploration of multiple independent directions simultaneously.
questions.question: What was the percentage performance improvement of the multi-agent system over single-agent Claude Opus 4?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that the multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on the internal research eval.

questions.lessonContent: To iterate on prompts, Anthropic had to understand their effects on agent behavior. They built simulations using their Console with the exact prompts and tools from their system, then watched agents work step-by-step. This approach immediately revealed failure modes: agents continuing when they already had sufficient results, using overly verbose search queries, or selecting incorrect tools. Effective prompting relies on developing an accurate mental model of the agent, which can make the most impactful changes obvious. The simulations allowed the team to identify specific issues like agents defaulting to overly long, specific queries that return few results.
questions.question: What did Anthropic build to help them understand the effects of prompts on agent behavior?
questions.answer: Simulations using their Console with the exact prompts and tools from their system, watching agents work step-by-step

questions.lessonContent: Research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. LLMs are a natural fit for grading outputs. Anthropic used an LLM judge that evaluated each output against criteria in a rubric: factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency. They experimented with multiple judges to evaluate each component, but found that a single LLM call with a single prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was the most consistent and aligned with human judgements.
questions.question: Anthropic found that using multiple LLM judges to evaluate each component of research outputs was more effective than using a single judge.

questions.lessonTitle: Scaling Effort Rules for Query Complexity
questions.lessonContent: Agents struggle to judge appropriate effort for different tasks, so Anthropic embedded scaling rules in the prompts. Simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These explicit guidelines help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently and prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was a common failure mode in early versions. The system also uses extended thinking mode where the lead agent uses thinking to plan its approach, assessing which tools fit the task, determining query complexity and subagent count.
questions.question: According to Anthropic's embedded scaling rules, how many subagents with how many tool calls are recommended for complex research tasks?
choices: More than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities, whereas simpler tasks use fewer agents and tool calls.

questions.lessonContent: To improve prompts effectively, we first need to understand how our agents behave. This requires building agent simulations to observe their actions step-by-step, which immediately reveals failure modes such as agents continuing when they already had sufficient results, using overly verbose search queries, or selecting incorrect tools. Once these failure modes are identified through simulation, we can iterate and improve prompts by addressing the specific issues discovered.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the prompt engineering iteration process for research agents?

questions.lessonTitle: Error Handling and Recovery in Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: In agentic systems, minor changes cascade into large behavioral changes, making it difficult to write code for complex agents that must maintain state in long-running processes. Agents can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls, which means errors need to be handled durably. Without effective mitigations, minor system failures can be catastrophic for agents because restarts are expensive and frustrating for users. To address this, engineers built systems that can resume from where the agent was when errors occurred, rather than restarting from the beginning. They also leverage the model's intelligence to handle issues gracefully by letting the agent know when a tool is failing and allowing it to adapt. This combines the adaptability of AI agents with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints.
questions.question: How do the agent systems handle errors to avoid costly restarts?
questions.answer: They built systems that can resume from where the agent was when errors occurred, combining AI adaptability with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and checkpoints.

questions.lessonContent: Agents make dynamic decisions and are non-deterministic between runs, even with identical prompts, which makes debugging harder. Users would report agents not finding obvious information, but engineers couldn't see whether agents were using bad search queries, choosing poor sources, or hitting tool failures. To diagnose why agents failed, the team added full production tracing that lets them see agent decision patterns and interaction structures without monitoring individual conversation contents. This high-level observability helped identify root causes, discover unexpected behaviors, and fix common failures systematically.
questions.question: True or false: The debugging approach for agents involves monitoring the contents of individual conversations to understand why agents fail.

questions.lessonTitle: Deployment Strategy for Stateful Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Agent systems are highly stateful webs of prompts, tools, and execution logic that run almost continuously. When deploying updates, agents might be anywhere in their process, so well-meaning code changes could break existing agents if they all receive the new version simultaneously. To prevent this disruption, the team uses rainbow deployments that gradually shift traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously. This allows the system to update incrementally without interrupting agents that are currently processing tasks, ensuring reliability during deployment transitions.
questions.question: What deployment strategy prevents disrupting running agents during updates?
choices: Rolling deployments that restart all agents simultaneously
Rainbow deployments that gradually shift traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running
Blue-green deployments that swap entire traffic at once
Canary deployments that redirect all traffic to the new version
questions.explanation: Rainbow deployments gradually shift traffic from old to new versions while keeping both running simultaneously, which prevents disrupting agents that may be in the middle of their process.

questions.lessonContent: In the multi-agent Research system, when a user submits a query, the lead agent begins by analyzing the query to understand the research requirements. After analysis, the lead agent saves its research plan to memory to preserve context and prevent loss if the context window exceeds 200,000 tokens. The lead agent then creates specialized subagents that explore different aspects of the topic in parallel.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-agent Research system's query processing workflow?

questions.lessonTitle: Context Length Capabilities of M2-BERT Retrieval Models
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers state-of-the-art long context M2-Retrieval models with varying context lengths to handle different document sizes. These models come in three context length options: 2k, 8k, and 32k tokens. This allows users to generate embeddings for long documents without splitting them into many short chunks while containing more meaningful contexts in the embeddings. The M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks, making them particularly useful for applications involving extensive text documents.
questions.question: What are the three context length options available for M2-BERT retrieval models in the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides 8 open source embedding models, including top models from the MTEB leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, as well as the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models. These models achieve state-of-the-art performance in MTEB, showing comparable or even better accuracies than closed models. Additionally, the M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models specifically in long context retrieval tasks. The pricing is also competitive, being up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms.
questions.question: M2-BERT retrieval models in the Together Embeddings endpoint significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks.

questions.lessonTitle: Available Embedding Models on the Platform
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers 8 open source embedding models for users to access. These include top models from the MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models. The platform also provides the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context applications (2k, 8k, 32k). All of these models are available through the Together API and can be accessed at very competitive prices. The endpoint includes models that outperform OpenAI's ada-002 and Cohere's Embed-v3 in both MTEB and LoCo Benchmarks.

To configure the client, you need to specify the Together API key and set the base URL to "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings". This endpoint structure enables seamless integration with existing codebases that use the OpenAI embeddings format.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides full OpenAI compatibility to facilitate migration for developers who have already built applications using the OpenAI API. This compatibility means that existing code designed for OpenAI's embeddings API can be switched to use Together's endpoint with minimal code changes, simply by updating the base URL and API key configuration.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers full OpenAI API compatibility, allowing developers to easily switch from OpenAI's embeddings API to Together's endpoint.

questions.lessonContent: Together Embeddings supports integration with multiple popular frameworks and databases for building Retrieval Augmented Generation applications. The available integrations include MongoDB for vector storage, LangChain for chaining language model components, and LlamaIndex for data indexing. These integrations enable developers to build RAG systems using their preferred tools while leveraging Together's embedding models.

Next, you define a get_embedding function that specifies the model and handles the text input. Finally, you call the embeddings.create method to generate embeddings for your text input. The correct sequence involves initializing the client, then defining the function, and finally making the API call.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Together Embeddings API integration process?

questions.lessonContent: Building a Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) system is one of the most popular use cases for embeddings models. You can build RAG using the Together API combined with popular vector databases such as MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma. These vector databases store and retrieve embeddings efficiently, enabling semantic search capabilities. The Together platform provides the embeddings while these databases handle the storage and retrieval aspects of the RAG pipeline.

The Together Embeddings endpoint can be used with popular frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex to construct RAG systems. These frameworks provide pre-built components for handling document loading, text splitting, embedding generation, and vector storage. Developers can choose either approach depending on their specific requirements and existing infrastructure.

questions.lessonContent: The dimension of embedding vectors is usually too large to easily visualize in its raw form. For the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model specifically, the embedding dimension is 768, which cannot be represented directly in a 2D plot. To plot each data example in two dimensions, the code uses t-SNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) to transform the high-dimensional embedding vectors into a lower-dimensional space suitable for visualization. The visualization uses sample data from various domains of RedPajama-v1 Sample, specifically from five data sources: arxiv_sample.jsonl, book_sample.jsonl, c4_sample.jsonl, github_sample.jsonl, and stackexchange_sample.jsonl. The code plots these using different colors for each data source and shows the average position for each source.

The first pair mentioned as closely related is github and stackexchange, which corresponds to choice index 0.

The document explicitly states that Kimi K2.5 is a 1.04T parameter model with 32B active parameters. This base model was selected after evaluating several potential open-source models including GLM-5 and DeepSeek V3.2, based on internal evaluations measuring coding knowledge, state tracking, and codebase perplexity.

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite designed to reflect real-world software engineering tasks. According to the document, CursorBench tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications compared to public benchmarks, with a median of 181 lines changed. The document explicitly compares this to public benchmarks which have only 7-10 lines changed. Additionally, CursorBench prompts are more under-specified with a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks.
questions.question: CursorBench tasks require a median of 181 lines changed, compared to 7-10 lines for public benchmarks like SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 achieves strong results on multiple evaluation suites. According to the results table, Composer 2 achieves 61.3% on CursorBench, 73.7% on SWE-bench Multilingual, and 61.7% on Terminal-Bench. These scores represent significant improvements over previous Composer versions, with a 37% relative improvement over Composer 1.5 on CursorBench. The document specifically notes that Composer 2's performance on these public benchmarks remains highly competitive with other state-of-the-art models.

questions.lessonContent: To enable Composer 2 to work across long horizons, the self-summarization technique is used where each training rollout can involve multiple generations chained together by summaries rather than a single prompt-response pair. The final reward is used for all tokens produced by the model in the chain, which upweights both the agent responses in good trajectories and also the self-summarizations that made them work. Poor summaries that lose critical information are downweighted during training. As Composer trains, it learns to use self-summaries to process more information even with a limited context window, and for hard examples it often self-summarizes multiple times.
questions.question: In the self-summarization technique used in Composer 2's RL training, how is the reward distributed across chained generations?
questions.answer: The final reward is applied to all tokens produced by the model in the chain

questions.lessonTitle: Handling Overlong Rollouts in RL Training
questions.lessonContent: Since agent rollouts can be very long, especially when aiming for long-horizon coherency, it is important that the system maintains stability in the highly asynchronous regime. Various prior works have employed masking of rollouts that exceed the maximum sequence length. However, the Composer 2 team did not see benefits with overlong masking at small scale and opted not to mask rollouts that exceed the maximum sequence length.
questions.question: Composer 2 opted NOT to mask rollouts that exceed the maximum sequence length during RL training.

questions.lessonTitle: Nonlinear Length Penalty for Efficient Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: To incentivize the model to produce solutions quickly on easy requests while allowing it to think longer on hard requests, a concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty is added to the reward. The formula is Clength{k,q}(x) = ((1 + kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1-q)), where k and q are hyperparameters defining the curvature, and x is a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns. The nonlinearity reflects that on easy tasks achievable with only a few tool calls, every additional bit of effort is felt more acutely than in long-horizon tasks where the agent might iterate for hundreds of tool calls.
questions.question: What behavior does the nonlinear length penalty incentivize the model to learn?
choices: Quick solutions on easy tasks and extended thinking on hard tasks
Longer thinking on all tasks regardless of difficulty
Shorter responses to reduce inference cost
Avoiding tool calls to minimize token usage
questions.explanation: The concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty specifically rewards the model for being efficient on easy tasks (quick solutions) while allowing more thinking time on hard tasks that require longer agent iterations.

questions.lessonTitle: Context Parallelism Configuration in Composer 2 Training
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses Context Parallelism (CP) as the primary long-context scaling axis, which requires less communication than Tensor Parallelism and improves compute efficiency by preserving full hidden dimensions in various projections. To implement CP efficiently in the Multi-Head Latent Attention architecture, the training team computes local KV latent vectors, all-gathers the latent vectors across CP ranks, and then computes the KV projections. They use EP=8, CP=2 for the continued pretraining phase and EP=8, CP=8 for the RL phase. This configuration allows the model to handle longer sequences effectively during training.
questions.question: What are the expert parallelism (EP) and context parallelism (CP) values used during the RL phase of Composer 2 training?

questions.lessonContent: The RL infrastructure uses router replay to address numerical differences between the inference engine forward pass and the trainer forward pass in Mixture-of-Experts models. Because Kimi K2.5 is a Mixture-of-Experts model, numerical differences can cause different experts to be chosen in the inference engine forward pass and trainer forward pass. If the trainer and inference engine do not agree on expert routing for each token, log-probabilities computed during training may not match the distribution from which tokens were sampled, introducing noise into the policy gradient. To address this, during inference, the engine returns the selected expert indices for every token at every MoE layer, and during the training forward pass the router's expert assignment is overridden to match. The router still computes gating scores so that gradients flow through it.
questions.question: Router replay is used in Composer 2's RL infrastructure to override the router's expert assignment during the training forward pass to match the inference engine's selected expert indices for every token at every MoE layer.

questions.lessonContent: Stateful codebase environments are a first-class artifact of the post-training stack, run on top of Anyrun, an internal compute platform built for running untrusted code at scale. Each Anyrun cluster is capable of scheduling more than 500 pods per second while maintaining desired binpacking requirements. The scheduling throughput is particularly important for the bursty nature of RL workloads. Within a cluster, a distributed set of Anyrun managers schedule pods, scale cloud compute provisioned across multiple regions, and perform state reconciliation to manage hundreds of thousands of pods per cluster.
questions.question: What is the maximum scheduling throughput that each Anyrun cluster is capable of handling?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that each Anyrun cluster is capable of scheduling more than 500 pods per second while maintaining desired binpacking requirements.

questions.lessonContent: CLAUDE.md is a special file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. This makes it an ideal place for documenting common bash commands, core files and utility functions, code style guidelines, testing instructions, repository etiquette, developer environment setup, and any unexpected behaviors or warnings particular to the project. You can place CLAUDE.md files in several locations including the root of your repo, any parent of the directory where you run claude, any child of that directory, or your home folder at ~/.claude/CLAUDE.md. When you want to keep a CLAUDE.md file private to your local environment and not share it with your team, you should name it CLAUDE.local.md and add it to your .gitignore file. The /init command will automatically generate a CLAUDE.md file for you.
questions.question: What is the recommended filename for a CLAUDE.md file that should be gitignored so it is not shared with your team?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code is intentionally low-level and unopinionated, providing close to raw model access without forcing specific workflows. By default, Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system, including file writes, many bash commands, and MCP tools. This deliberate conservative approach prioritizes safety over convenience. You can customize the allowlist to permit additional tools that you know are safe, or to allow potentially unsafe tools that are easy to undo such as file editing or git commit. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: selecting "Always allow" when prompted, using the /permissions command, manually editing your .claude/settings.json file, or using the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: Claude Code was designed with a deliberately conservative approach to tool permissions by default.

questions.lessonTitle: Managing Allowed Tools in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code provides four distinct methods for managing which tools are allowed to run without prompting for permission. The first method is to select "Always allow" when prompted during a session whenever Claude requests permission for an action. The second method involves using the /permissions command after starting Claude Code, which allows you to add or remove tools from the allowlist, such as adding Edit to always allow file edits or Bash(git commit:*) to allow git commits. The third method is to manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json files, with the former recommended for checking into source control to share with your team. The fourth method uses the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions that apply only to the current session.
questions.question: What are the four ways to manage allowed tools in Claude Code?
choices: Only use the /permissions command and the --allowedTools CLI flag
Manually edit .claude/settings.json, use the /permissions command, or ask Claude verbally
Add tools to your CLAUDE.md file, use the /permissions command, edit settings.json, or restart Claude Code
Select "Always allow" when prompted during a session, use the /permissions command, manually edit .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json, and use the --allowedTools CLI flag
questions.explanation: The four ways to manage allowed tools are: 1) Select "Always allow" when prompted during a session, 2) Use the /permissions command to add or remove tools, 3) Manually edit .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json, and 4) Use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.

questions.lessonContent: When customizing your Claude Code setup, the process follows a logical sequence. First, you must create CLAUDE.md files, which are special files that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. Second, you should tune your CLAUDE.md files by refining them like any frequently used prompt, taking time to experiment and determine what produces the best instruction following from the model. Third, you curate Claude's list of allowed tools by customizing the allowlist to permit additional tools that you know are safe, or to allow potentially unsafe tools that are easy to undo.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in customizing your Claude Code environment?

questions.lessonTitle: Thinking Modes in Claude Code Workflows
questions.lessonContent: In the 'Explore, plan, code, commit' workflow, you can ask Claude to make a plan using the word 'think' to trigger extended thinking mode. This gives Claude additional computation time to evaluate alternatives more thoroughly. The specific phrases are mapped directly to increasing levels of thinking budget: 'think' provides the smallest budget, followed by 'think hard', then 'think harder', and finally 'ultrathink' which allocates the most thinking budget for Claude to use.
questions.question: What is the order of increasing thinking budget when using the 'think' command in Claude Code?
questions.answer: think < think hard < think harder < ultrathink

questions.lessonTitle: Image Input Methods in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude can work with images and diagrams through several methods. You can paste screenshots directly into the prompt input, with a pro tip for macOS users to hit cmd+ctrl+shift+4 to screenshot to clipboard and then ctrl+v to paste. You can also drag and drop images directly into the prompt input, or provide file paths for images so Claude can read them.
questions.question: True or false: On macOS, you can screenshot to clipboard using cmd+v to paste into Claude Code.

questions.lessonTitle: Course Correction Tools in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: When working with Claude Code, you can guide and correct Claude's approach at any time using several tools. You can ask Claude to make a plan before coding and explicitly tell it not to code until you've confirmed the plan. Pressing Escape interrupts Claude during any phase—thinking, tool calls, or file edits—while preserving context so you can redirect or expand instructions. Double-tapping Escape lets you jump back in history, edit a previous prompt, and explore a different direction. You can also ask Claude to undo changes to take a different approach.
questions.question: What is the correct way to interrupt Claude Code while preserving context for redirection?
choices: Press Escape to interrupt and preserve context
Press Ctrl+C to stop and lose context
questions.explanation: Pressing Escape interrupts Claude during any phase—thinking, tool calls, or file edits—while preserving context so you can redirect or expand instructions.

questions.lessonContent: The 'Explore, plan, code, commit' workflow is a versatile pattern for solving many problems with Claude Code. First, explore by asking Claude to read relevant files, images, or URLs - provide general or specific filenames but explicitly tell it not to write any code yet. Next, ask Claude to make a plan for how to approach the problem using the word 'think' to trigger extended thinking mode. If the results seem reasonable, you can have Claude create a document or GitHub issue with its plan. Then, ask Claude to implement its solution in code while verifying reasonableness as it implements pieces of the solution. Finally, ask Claude to commit the result and create a pull request.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the 'Explore, plan, code, commit' workflow for solving problems with Claude Code?
choices: Ask Claude to make a plan

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. To enable headless mode, you use the -p flag with a prompt. Additionally, you can use --output-format stream-json for streaming JSON output. It's important to note that headless mode does not persist between sessions—you have to trigger it each session.
questions.question: What command line flag is used to enable headless mode in Claude Code?

questions.lessonContent: Claude Code's headless mode is designed for non-interactive contexts such as CI pipelines, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and various automation tasks. The mode allows Claude to operate without user interaction by providing a prompt directly through the command line.
questions.question: True or false: Headless mode in Claude Code persists between sessions automatically.

questions.lessonContent: Beyond standalone usage, some of the most powerful applications involve running multiple Claude instances in parallel. There are several strategies for this: one Claude can write code while another verifies the work in a separate terminal. Another approach is creating multiple git checkouts in separate folders and opening each folder in separate terminal tabs. Additionally, git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, each with its own working directory while sharing the same Git history and reflog.
questions.question: Which of the following is a valid approach for running multiple Claude instances in parallel?
choices: Creating multiple git checkouts in separate folders and opening each in separate terminal tabs
Having one Claude write code while another verifies in a separate terminal
Running Claude in headless mode with a custom harness for automated tasks
Using git worktrees to check out multiple branches into separate directories
questions.explanation: Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, enabling multiple Claude sessions simultaneously on different parts of your project.

questions.lessonContent: When using Claude Code in headless mode for large-scale migrations like moving files from one framework to another, the process involves multiple steps. First, you define a migration task list by having Claude write a script to generate tasks. Then you loop through tasks programmatically by calling Claude for each task and giving it specific tools to use. Each invocation should return either the string OK if it succeeded or FAIL if the task failed. After running the script several times, you refine your prompt to get the desired outcome.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the headless mode migration workflow?
choices: Call Claude with task and tools

results.file: How does image compression work_ _ Lee Robinson.pdf

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Images and Compression Fundamentals
questions.lessonContent: Images look smooth and continuous, but when you zoom in far enough, you'll see they're made of tiny colored squares called pixels. Each pixel contains three numbers representing how much red, green, and blue to mix together to create that specific color. Each of these color values ranges from 0, representing no color, to 255, representing maximum intensity. For example, a pixel with RGB values of (255, 147, 41) would appear orange. This RGB color model is the foundation of how digital images represent color.
questions.question: What are the three color components that make up each pixel?

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Images and Compression Fundamentals
questions.lessonContent: Lossless compression is one of two main approaches to reducing file size while preserving image quality. PNG is a format that uses lossless compression, which means it preserves every single pixel perfectly while still shrinking the file size. This is different from lossy compression, which throws away data that humans won't notice. Lossless compression is particularly useful for screenshots with text or graphics with sharp edges where every pixel must be exact. The three main tricks used in lossless compression are filtering, pattern-finding with LZ77, and Huffman coding.
questions.question: PNG uses lossless compression to preserve every single pixel.

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Images and Compression Fundamentals
questions.lessonContent: To understand why compression is necessary, consider an HD screenshot with dimensions of 1920 × 1080 pixels. Multiplying these together gives over 2 million pixels (2,073,600 to be exact). Since each pixel needs 3 bytes to store the red, green, and blue values, the raw file size would be approximately 6.2 megabytes for a single image. Without compression, this would make images impractical for web use and storage. Using lossless compression techniques like those in PNG, a 6.2 MB photograph can be reduced to around 2.1 MB, achieving roughly 3 times smaller file size with zero quality loss.
questions.question: How many pixels does a 1920 × 1080 HD image contain?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that 1920 × 1080 equals 2,073,600 pixels, which when multiplied by 3 bytes equals 6,220,800 bytes (approximately 6.2 MB).

questions.moduleTitle: Introduction to Images and Compression Fundamentals
questions.lessonContent: In PNG compression, the process begins with Apply Filtering to store differences between pixels rather than actual values. Next, LZ77 Pattern Finding identifies and replaces repeated sequences with compact back-references. Finally, Huffman Encoding assigns shorter binary codes to values that appear more frequently, significantly reducing file size.
questions.question: What is the correct order of the compression stages in PNG image compression?

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Visual Perception
questions.lessonContent: JPEG exploits a specific characteristic of human vision to achieve compression. Your eyes resolve brightness in fine detail but blur color together. You notice a blurry edge, but you won't notice if colors are slightly off. JPEG converts pixels from RGB to a different format that separates brightness from color. It also reduces color resolution since your eyes won't notice the difference. This allows JPEG to discard color information while preserving the perceived visual quality of the image.
questions.question: What aspect of human vision does JPEG exploit to reduce color resolution?
questions.answer: Human eyes blur color together but resolve brightness in fine detail

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Visual Perception
questions.lessonContent: After converting RGB to a format that separates brightness from color, JPEG divides the image into 8×8 pixel blocks and transforms each block into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients while high frequencies represent fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs are mostly smooth gradients, most of the information ends up in just a few low-frequency components. JPEG throws away the high-frequency details you won't miss, keeping the smooth parts intact.
questions.question: JPEG preserves low-frequency components and discards high-frequency components in an image.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Visual Perception
questions.lessonContent: JPEG is a lossy compression format that achieves significant file size reduction. With lossy compression, you cannot get the original pixels back once the compression is applied. However, the trade-off is often worth it: JPEG can achieve 10-20x smaller files with minimal visible difference at high quality settings. At high quality, you barely notice the difference. But when compression is cranked up, you'll see blocking artifacts where fine details get lost. Unlike PNG, JPEG does not support alpha (transparency), which is one reason PNG is preferred for graphics with transparency.
questions.question: Which of the following is a characteristic of JPEG compression compared to lossless formats?
choices: JPEG preserves all original color information without loss
JPEG cannot recover the original pixels after compression
JPEG produces smaller files than PNG for all image types
questions.explanation: JPEG is a lossy format, meaning once compression is applied, the original pixel data cannot be recovered. This is the fundamental trade-off for achieving 10-20x file size reduction.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Visual Perception
questions.lessonTitle: Lossy Compression: JPEG and Visual Perception
questions.lessonContent: In JPEG compression, the process of transforming image data involves several key steps. First, the image is divided into 8x8 pixel blocks. Then, each block undergoes a mathematical transformation that converts pixel values into frequency components. Low frequencies represent smooth gradients in the image, while high frequencies capture fine details like sharp edges. Since photographs contain mostly smooth gradients, most information exists in just a few low-frequency components.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the block-based frequency transformation process of JPEG compression?

questions.moduleTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG, Filtering, and Encoding
questions.lessonTitle: PNG Filtering Methods and Their Best Use Cases
questions.lessonContent: PNG uses a technique called filtering or prediction to compress images. Instead of storing the actual pixel values, PNG stores how much each pixel differs from its predicted value based on neighboring pixels. PNG supports four prediction methods: Sub (predicts from the left neighbor), Up (predicts from the pixel above), Average (predicts from the average of left and above), and Paeth (intelligently picks between left, above, or diagonal). PNG encoders try each method per row and select the one that achieves the best compression for that specific row of data.
questions.question: Which PNG filtering method works best for horizontal gradients?

questions.moduleTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG, Filtering, and Encoding
questions.lessonContent: PNG is the preferred format for graphics with transparency because it supports an alpha channel, which represents transparency values. While standard RGB uses 3 bytes per pixel (red, green, and blue), RGBA uses 4 bytes per pixel to include the alpha transparency channel. This allows for varying levels of transparency in an image, from fully opaque to fully transparent. In contrast, JPEG does not support alpha channels, making PNG necessary for images that require transparency.
questions.question: PNG supports alpha transparency, but JPEG does not.

questions.moduleTitle: Lossless Compression: PNG, Filtering, and Encoding
questions.lessonContent: PNG combines three compression techniques in sequence to reduce file size while preserving all pixel data. First, filtering stores differences between pixels rather than absolute values, making the data more compressible. Second, LZ77 scans for repeated patterns in a sliding window of 32 KB and replaces them with back-references to previously seen data. Third, Huffman coding assigns shorter binary codes to more frequently occurring values. The compressed data is then wrapped in PNG format chunks with headers and checksums (CRC-32) for error detection.
questions.question: What is the correct order of the compression stages in PNG image compression?
questions.explanation: The correct pipeline is: Filtering (predict from neighbors), then LZ77 (find repeated patterns), then Huffman (shorter codes for common values), and finally wrap in PNG format with headers and checksums.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Rise and Peak of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: There were two periods of Roman government. The Roman Republic lasted from 509 BCE to 30 BCE. The Roman Empire began after the Roman Republic ended, specifically from 30 BCE to 476 CE. While Rome technically had an empire under the Roman Republic, the term Roman Empire refers to the time period beginning with Augustus when Rome was ruled by emperors. The transition from Republic to Empire occurred when Octavian became the sole ruler of Rome after defeating Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium.
questions.question: What are the dates of the Roman Empire?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Rise and Peak of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Octavian was sole ruler of Rome after his forces defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium. The Senate gave him the name Augustus, which means most high. In 23 BCE, Octavian, now referred to as Augustus, was made consul for life by the Senate. He was also made Princeps, meaning first citizen, which is the origin of the word prince. Additionally, he was made Imperator, meaning successful general, which is the origin of the word emperor.
questions.question: The Senate gave Octavian the name Augustus, meaning most high.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Rise and Peak of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Claudius became emperor in 41 CE because he was the last adult male of his family. He was the brother of Germanicus and uncle of Caligula. During his reign, Claudius brought southern Britannia, which later became Great Britain, under Roman control. He also brought several kingdoms in the East under Roman control. Claudius opened the Senate up to provincials, allowing people from the provinces to become senators. He conducted a census of the empire in 48 CE.
questions.question: Which Roman emperor brought southern Britannia under Roman control?
questions.explanation: Claudius brought southern Britannia under Roman control, as well as several kingdoms in the East. He became emperor because he was the last adult male of his family.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 1: Rise and Peak of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonTitle: Rise and Peak of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The transformation of Octavian into Augustus marked a crucial turning point in Roman history. First, Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at the Battle of Actium, establishing himself as sole ruler of Rome. Next, the Senate gave him the name "Augustus," meaning "most high," which elevated his status above other Roman leaders. Finally, in 23 BCE, Octavian was made consul for life by the Senate, granting him permanent political power and solidifying his position as the first Roman emperor.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the rise of Augustus to power?

questions.lessonTitle: The Principle of Primus Inter Pares
questions.lessonContent: The Latin phrase "primus inter pares" means "first among equals." Augustus and later Roman emperors tried to maintain the façade that they were elected officials rather than dictators. Being "first among equals" gave the illusion that an emperor was the most prestigious and important member of the Roman Senate, but that each senator was simultaneously equally important. In reality, the Roman emperors ruled with little input from anyone else. This principle was a political fiction designed to maintain the appearance of republican governance while consolidating imperial power.
questions.question: What does the Latin phrase "primus inter pares" mean?

questions.lessonTitle: The Division of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms (east and west) in 285 CE. This was the first step in the creation of what would become two separate empires: the Roman (Western) Empire and the Byzantine (Eastern) Empire. Diocletian believed that dividing the empire for administrative purposes would strengthen it. However, once Constantine set up Constantinople as a capital city, the east/west split deepened rather than strengthened the empire.
questions.question: Diocletian divided the empire into eastern and western administrative halves in 285 CE.

questions.lessonContent: Constantine had a significant relationship with Christianity through his mother Helena, who had converted to the religion. The Edict of Milan in 313 CE legalized Christianity and established religious toleration throughout the empire. Constantine converted to Christianity on his deathbed. Under Constantine, Christianity finally gained acceptance, and future Roman emperors were Christians. This marked a major transformation in the religious landscape of the Roman Empire.
questions.question: Which emperor issued the Edict of Milan in 313 CE, legalizing Christianity?
questions.explanation: Constantine issued the Edict of Milan in 313 CE, which legalized Christianity and established religious toleration throughout the Roman Empire.

questions.lessonTitle: Transformation and Division of the Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The process of dividing the Roman Empire into Eastern and Western halves began when Emperor Diocletian divided the empire into two administrative realms in 285 CE, creating separate East/West Administration to improve governance. This administrative division was further strengthened when Constantine moved the capital from Rome to Byzantium, renaming it Constantinople. These actions laid the groundwork for the eventual permanent split between the Western Roman Empire and the Eastern Byzantine Empire.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the division of the Roman Empire into East and West?

questions.lessonTitle: End of the Western Roman Empire
questions.lessonContent: The Western Roman Empire ended officially in 476 CE when the last emperor, Romulus Augustus, was deposed by a barbarian named Odoacer. This event marks the traditional date for the fall of the Roman Empire in the West. The Eastern Roman Empire, also known as the Byzantine Empire, continued to exist for nearly another millennium. The Byzantine Empire lasted until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. The fall of the Western Roman Empire was the result of multiple factors including economic troubles, military instability, political chaos, and social decline.
questions.question: When did the Western Roman Empire officially end?

questions.lessonContent: The Eastern Roman Empire, also known as the Byzantine Empire, was established after the division of the Roman Empire under Diocletian in 285 CE. While the Western Roman Empire fell in 476 CE, the Eastern Empire continued to thrive for many centuries. Constantinople served as the capital of the Byzantine Empire and became a major center of Christianity and learning. The Byzantine Empire lasted until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks. This conquest marked the final end of the Roman Empire that had begun with Augustus centuries earlier.
questions.question: The Eastern (Byzantine) Empire lasted until 1453 when it was conquered by the Ottoman Turks.

questions.lessonContent: Emperor Justinian ruled the Byzantine Empire from 527 to 565 CE and accomplished several significant things during his reign. He managed to temporarily reunite the Eastern and Western empires, though this reunification did not last. Justinian rewrote Roman law in what became known as the Corpus Juris Civilis or the Justinian Code, which still serves as the basis for civil law in several countries today. However, his reign was also marked by a devastating pandemic known as the Plague of Justinian, which occurred in 541-542 CE. This bubonic plague severely hurt the Byzantine empire, causing Emperor Justinian himself to become sick, though he eventually recovered. The recovery for the Byzantine empire took hundreds of years.
questions.question: When did the Plague of Justinian occur?
questions.explanation: The Plague of Justinian specifically occurred in 541-542 CE, as stated in the source content. It was a bubonic plague that severely hurt the Byzantine empire during Justinian's reign.

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.moduleTitle: Foundations and Benefits of Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents, which are large language models autonomously using tools in a loop, working together to accomplish tasks. The Research feature involves an agent that plans a research process based on user queries and then uses tools to create parallel agents that search for information simultaneously. This architectural approach allows different subagents to explore different aspects of a question at the same time before condensing their findings for the lead research agent. Systems with multiple agents introduce new challenges in agent coordination, evaluation, and reliability that must be carefully managed.
questions.question: What is a multi-agent system?
questions.answer: A multi-agent system consists of multiple agents (LLMs autonomously using tools in a loop) working together

questions.moduleTitle: Foundations and Benefits of Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonTitle: Performance Gains of Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: Our internal evaluations show that multi-agent research systems excel especially for breadth-first queries that involve pursuing multiple independent directions simultaneously. We conducted experiments where a multi-agent system used Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents. This multi-agent configuration was compared against a single-agent Claude Opus 4 system on the same internal research evaluation. The results demonstrated that the multi-agent system significantly outperformed the single-agent system in its ability to decompose complex queries into tasks for parallel subagents.
questions.question: The multi-agent system with Claude Opus 4 as lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on the internal research eval.

questions.moduleTitle: Foundations and Benefits of Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonTitle: Primary Factor Explaining Performance Variance in Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: In our analysis of the BrowseComp evaluation, which tests the ability of browsing agents to locate hard-to-find information, we examined what factors explained performance variance. We found that three factors together explained 95% of the performance variance: token usage, number of tool calls, and model choice. However, token usage by itself explained 80% of the variance, making it the dominant factor. This finding validates the multi-agent architecture that distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add more capacity for parallel reasoning. The architecture effectively scales token usage for tasks that exceed the limits of single agents.
questions.question: Which single factor explains the highest percentage of performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, which is the highest single factor among the three explanatory factors (token usage, number of tool calls, and model choice).

questions.lessonContent: The Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The subagents act as intelligent filters by iteratively using search tools to gather information before returning their findings to the lead agent. This architecture differs from traditional Retrieval Augmented Generation approaches by using dynamic multi-step search that adapts to new findings rather than static retrieval.
questions.question: What architectural pattern does the Research system use for multi-agent coordination?

questions.lessonTitle: Research System Workflow and Citation Generation
questions.lessonContent: The complete research workflow involves several sequential steps: when a user submits a query, the system creates a LeadResearcher agent that enters an iterative research process. The LeadResearcher begins by thinking through the approach and saving its plan to Memory to persist context, since if the context window exceeds 200,000 tokens it will be truncated. It then creates specialized Subagents with specific research tasks, and each Subagent independently performs web searches, evaluates tool results using interleaved thinking, and returns findings. Once sufficient information is gathered, the system passes all findings to a CitationAgent, which processes the documents to identify specific locations for citations. The final research results with citations are then returned to the user.
questions.question: In the Research system workflow, the CitationAgent identifies specific locations for citations.

questions.lessonTitle: Token Usage Comparison Across System Types
questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems consume significantly more tokens than single-agent systems. In practice, agents typically use about 4 times more tokens than chat interactions, while multi-agent systems use about 15 times more tokens than standard chats. This high token consumption means multi-agent systems require tasks where the value is high enough to justify the increased costs. The architecture distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add capacity for parallel reasoning, and this approach works best for valuable tasks involving heavy parallelization, information that exceeds single context windows, and interfacing with numerous complex tools.
questions.question: What is the approximate token usage ratio of multi-agent systems compared to standard chat interactions?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats.

questions.lessonTitle: Principles of Prompt Engineering for Multi-Agent Systems
questions.lessonContent: Prompt engineering serves as the primary lever for improving multi-agent behaviors. Early agents made errors like spawning 50 subagents for simple queries, scouring the web endlessly for nonexistent sources, and distracting each other with excessive updates. One key principle is scaling effort to query complexity: simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. Another principle teaches the orchestrator how to delegate by providing each subagent with an objective, an output format, guidance on tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries. Additionally, agents should start with short, broad queries before progressively narrowing focus, rather than defaulting to overly long, specific queries that return few results.
questions.question: According to the prompt engineering principles, how many subagents and tool calls are recommended for simple fact-finding tasks versus complex research tasks?
questions.answer: Simple fact-finding requires 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls; complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities

questions.lessonContent: Research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. LLMs are a natural fit for grading outputs. An LLM judge evaluates each output against criteria in a rubric: factual accuracy (do claims match sources?), citation accuracy (do the cited sources match the claims?), completeness (are all requested aspects covered?), source quality (did it use primary sources over lower-quality secondary sources?), and tool efficiency (did it use the right tools a reasonable number of times?). The most effective approach uses a single LLM call with a single prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade, which proved most consistent and aligned with human judgments. This method was especially effective when eval test cases had a clear answer.
questions.question: In the LLM-as-judge evaluation approach described, the judge evaluates outputs against multiple criteria including factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency.

questions.lessonTitle: Agent Error Handling and Recovery Strategies
questions.lessonContent: In agentic systems, minor changes cascade into large behavioral changes, making it remarkably difficult to write code for complex agents that must maintain state in a long-running process. Agents can run for long periods of time, maintaining state across many tool calls, which means errors compound. When errors occur, restarts are expensive and frustrating for users, so they built systems that can resume from where the agent was when errors occurred. They also combine the adaptability of AI agents built on Claude with deterministic safeguards like retry logic and regular checkpoints. Additionally, they use the model's intelligence to handle issues gracefully by letting the agent know when a tool is failing and letting it adapt, which works surprisingly well.
questions.question: Which evaluation approach is used for agentic systems that have free-form text outputs and rarely have a single correct answer?
choices: LLM-as-judge with a rubric evaluating factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, and tool efficiency
Rule-based evaluation checking specific output formats
Automated programmatic evaluation checking exact string matches
questions.explanation: The LLM-as-judge approach is specifically designed for free-form text outputs. It uses an LLM to evaluate against criteria like factual accuracy and source quality, outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 with a pass-fail grade.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint was released on January 11, 2024, and is available with 8 open source embedding models. These include top models from the MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) leaderboard such as UAE-Large-v1 and BGE models, as well as the newly released M2-BERT retrieval models for long context with context lengths of 2k, 8k, and 32k. The endpoint offers state-of-the-art performance in MTEB, showing comparable or even better accuracies than closed models. Additionally, M2-BERT retrieval models significantly outperform other closed models in long context retrieval tasks. The endpoint is also up to 4x cheaper than other popular platforms.
questions.question: What is the maximum context length available for the M2-BERT retrieval models?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint is fully OpenAI compatible, allowing users who have already built applications following the OpenAI API to easily switch to Together's endpoint. Users can configure the client by specifying the base URL as "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings" while using the same OpenAI client initialization pattern. The API string for one of the models is "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-32k-retrieval". This compatibility makes migration straightforward for existing applications.
questions.question: The Together Embeddings endpoint is fully OpenAI compatible, making migration easy for existing applications.

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint offers models that outperform both OpenAI's ada-002 and Cohere's Embed-v3 in MTEB and LoCo Benchmarks. The endpoint includes integrations with MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex for RAG applications. For the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model specifically, the embedding dimension is 768. Text embeddings provide a measure of the similarity or relatedness of given text queries, and they are used for applications including clustering, semantic search, and classification, as well as retrieval augmented generation (RAG).
questions.question: What is the embedding dimension for the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly states that for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K, the embedding dimension is 768.

questions.lessonTitle: Ordering Steps in Embedding Visualization Process
questions.lessonContent: In the data visualization example using the Together Embeddings endpoint, the process begins by sampling data and generating embeddings through the sample_and_extract_embeddings function, which calls generate_embeddings internally. Next, the high-dimensional embedding vectors are reduced to 2D using the transform_tSNE function, as embedding dimensions (768 for M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K) are too large to visualize directly. Finally, the transformed embeddings are plotted using the plot_embeddings function and displayed with plt.show().
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the embedding visualization workflow using the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint is configured using a base URL of "https://api.together.xyz/api/v1/embeddings". To use this endpoint, you initialize the OpenAI client with your Together API key and set the base URL to this endpoint. The client can then create embeddings by calling the embeddings.create method with input text and the model parameter. The model parameter requires the specific API string for the embedding model, such as "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-32k-retrieval" for the 32k context model. This OpenAI-compatible approach allows for straightforward integration into existing applications.
questions.question: What is the base URL required to configure the Together Embeddings endpoint when using OpenAI compatibility?

questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint supports integration with popular frameworks and databases for building RAG applications. Specifically, the documentation mentions integrations with MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex. These integrations allow developers to build RAG systems using Together API combined with vector databases like MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma. The platform provides tutorials for implementing RAG with each of these frameworks, enabling flexible options for semantic search and retrieval augmented generation use cases.
questions.question: True or False: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides integrations with MongoDB, LangChain, and LlamaIndex for building RAG applications.

questions.lessonTitle: Model API String Format for Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: When making API calls to the Together Embeddings endpoint, you must specify the model using its exact API string. The API string format follows a specific pattern for each model. For example, the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model uses the API string "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval", while the 32k context version uses "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-32k-retrieval". These strings are used directly in the model parameter when calling the embeddings.create method to generate embeddings for your text inputs.
questions.question: What is the correct API string for the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model?
questions.explanation: The correct API string uses the format "togethercomputer/m2-bert-80M-8k-retrieval" which includes the vendor prefix "togethercomputer/", followed by the model name "m2-bert", the parameter count "80M", and the context length "8k" with the model type "retrieval".

questions.lessonTitle: API Client Setup for Together Embeddings
questions.lessonContent: When setting up the Together Embeddings endpoint with OpenAI compatibility, you first need to create an OpenAI client by initializing it with your Together API key and specifying the Together base URL. Next, you define a helper function that uses this client to generate embeddings by calling the embeddings.create method with your text input and chosen model. Finally, you make the actual embedding request by calling your defined function with the text you want to embed.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in setting up an OpenAI-compatible client for the Together Embeddings endpoint?

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is a technique that addresses critical limitations of generative AI models. One major limitation is the lack of knowledge from unseen data, which means models cannot access information they weren't trained on. RAG overcomes this by using embeddings to find relevant information from a given knowledge base, then providing that information to a generative model. This allows the system to generate responses that incorporate information beyond the model's original training data, making the output more accurate and grounded in specific domain knowledge.
questions.question: What limitation of generative AI models does RAG primarily aim to overcome?
questions.answer: lack of knowledge from unseen data

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: Embedding vectors typically have dimensions that are too large to easily visualize in their raw form. For example, the M2-BERT-Retrieval-8K model produces embedding vectors with 768 dimensions. To plot these high-dimensional embeddings in 2D for visualization, tSNE (t-distributed Stochastic Neighbor Embedding) is used as a transformation technique. The transformation reduces the dimensionality while preserving the relative relationships between data points, allowing users to see clusters and patterns in the embedding space.
questions.question: True or False: tSNE is used to reduce embedding dimensions from 768 to 2 for visualization.

questions.moduleTitle: Building RAG Applications and Data Visualization
questions.lessonContent: The Together Embeddings endpoint provides integrations with popular frameworks for building RAG applications. Specifically, developers can build RAG systems using Together API alongside frameworks such as LangChain and LlamaIndex, or with vector databases including MongoDB, Pinecone, and Chroma. These integrations simplify the process of connecting embedding generation with retrieval systems, allowing developers to leverage their preferred tools while using the Together Embeddings endpoint for generating text embeddings.
questions.question: Which framework integration is NOT mentioned for building RAG with Together Embeddings?
questions.explanation: The content explicitly mentions LangChain and LlamaIndex as framework integrations for building RAG. MongoDB is also mentioned as a vector database integration. HuggingFace is not mentioned anywhere in the source content as an integration for building RAG with Together Embeddings.

questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 is a specialized model designed for agentic software engineering, demonstrating strong long-term planning and coding intelligence while maintaining the ability to efficiently solve problems for interactive use. The model scores strongly on CursorBench, a benchmark of real-world software engineering, while also scoring at frontier levels on public software engineering benchmarks such as SWE-bench Multilingual and Terminal-Bench. The model is trained in two phases: first, continued pretraining to improve the model's knowledge and latent coding ability, followed by large-scale reinforcement learning to improve end-to-end coding performance.
