questions.moduleTitle: Module 3: The Enduring Legacy of Roman Civilization
questions.lessonContent: Emperor Justinian (527-565 CE) was a powerful ruler of the Eastern Byzantine Empire who rewrote Roman law into the Corpus Juris Civilis, also known as the Justinian Code. This legal code still serves as the basis for civil law in several European countries. Justinian also married Theodora, an intelligent courtesan, and managed to reunite the Eastern and Western empires for a time, though this reunification did not last.
questions.question: Which of the following is an accomplishment of Emperor Justinian?
choices: Rewriting Roman law into the Justinian Code
questions.explanation: Emperor Justinian rewrote Roman law into the Corpus Juris Civilis (the Justinian Code), which still serves as the basis for civil law in several European countries. The Colosseum was built by Emperor Vespasian, not Justinian. The Pax Romana was established under Augustus, and while Justinian did reunite the Eastern and Western empires temporarily, he did not conquer the Persian Empire.

results.file: How we built our multi-agent research system _ Anthropic.pdf

questions.lessonContent: Our Research system uses a multi-agent architecture with an orchestrator-worker pattern, where a lead agent coordinates the process while delegating to specialized subagents that operate in parallel. When a user submits a query, the lead agent analyzes it, develops a strategy, and spawns subagents to explore different aspects simultaneously. The subagents act as intelligent filters by iteratively using search tools to gather information and then returning a list of results to the lead agent so it can compile a final answer. This architecture enables the system to handle complex, open-ended research tasks that require dynamic adaptation.
questions.question: What architecture pattern does the Anthropic Research system use?

questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems consume significantly more tokens than single-agent systems. In the data from Anthropic, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, and multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. This high token usage is necessary for the increased performance these systems provide, but it creates economic considerations. For multi-agent systems to be economically viable, the tasks must be valuable enough to justify the increased computational cost.
questions.question: Multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chat interactions.

questions.lessonContent: In their analysis of the BrowseComp evaluation, which tests the ability of browsing agents to locate hard-to-find information, Anthropic found that three factors explained 95% of the performance variance. Token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, making it the dominant factor. The number of tool calls and the model choice were the two other explanatory factors. This finding validates their architecture that distributes work across agents with separate context windows to add more capacity for parallel reasoning.
questions.question: According to the source content, what factor explains 80% of the performance variance in the BrowseComp evaluation?
questions.explanation: Token usage by itself explains 80% of the variance, with the number of tool calls and model choice as the other two factors explaining the remaining 15%.

questions.lessonContent: In the multi-agent research system workflow, when a user submits a query, the lead agent first analyzes it and develops a strategy. The LeadResearcher then creates specialized subagents with specific research tasks. Finally, these Subagents Search Parallel by independently performing web searches and returning findings to the lead agent.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in Anthropic's multi-agent research system workflow?

questions.lessonTitle: Performance Gains in Multi-Agent Research Systems
questions.lessonContent: Our internal evaluations demonstrate that multi-agent research systems excel especially for breadth-first queries involving multiple independent directions. Testing showed that a multi-agent system using Claude Opus 4 as the lead agent and Claude Sonnet 4 subagents outperformed a single-agent Claude Opus 4 by 90.2% on our internal research evaluation. For example, when asked to identify all board members of companies in the Information Technology S&P 500, the multi-agent system succeeded by decomposing the task into parallel subagent searches, while the single-agent system failed with slow, sequential searches.
questions.question: What percentage improvement did the multi-agent system (Claude Opus 4 lead with Claude Sonnet 4 subagents) achieve over single-agent Claude Opus 4 on the internal research evaluation?

questions.lessonContent: In multi-agent systems, the lead agent must effectively decompose queries into subtasks and communicate them clearly to subagents. Each subagent needs an objective, an output format, guidance on which tools and sources to use, and clear task boundaries. Without detailed task descriptions, agents duplicate work, leave gaps, or fail to find necessary information. We started by allowing the lead agent to give simple, short instructions like 'research the semiconductor shortage,' but found these instructions were often vague enough that subagents misinterpreted the task or performed identical searches. For instance, one subagent explored the 2021 automotive chip crisis while two others duplicated work investigating current 2025 supply chains.
questions.question: When the lead agent gave simple, short instructions like 'research the semiconductor shortage' without detailed task descriptions, subagents sometimes explored completely different topics, such as one investigating the 2021 automotive chip crisis while others investigated current 2025 supply chains.

questions.lessonTitle: Scaling Guidelines Based on Query Complexity
questions.lessonContent: Agents struggle to judge appropriate effort for different tasks, so scaling rules must be embedded in prompts. Simple fact-finding requires just one agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents with clearly divided responsibilities. These explicit guidelines help the lead agent allocate resources efficiently and prevent overinvestment in simple queries, which was a common failure mode in early versions.
questions.question: According to the source content, which of the following represents the correct scaling guideline for effort allocation based on query complexity?
choices: Simple fact-finding requires 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, complex research uses more than 10 subagents
Simple fact-finding requires 2-3 agents with 5-10 tool calls, direct comparisons need 3-5 subagents with 15-20 calls each, complex research uses 5-10 subagents
Simple fact-finding requires 3 agents with 10-15 tool calls, direct comparisons need 5-7 subagents with 20-30 calls each, complex research uses 15+ subagents
Simple fact-finding requires 1 subagent with 1-5 tool calls, direct comparisons need 1-2 subagents with 5-10 calls each, complex research uses 3-5 subagents
questions.explanation: The source explicitly states that simple fact-finding requires just 1 agent with 3-10 tool calls, direct comparisons might need 2-4 subagents with 10-15 calls each, and complex research might use more than 10 subagents.

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic's engineering team developed a systematic approach to evaluating multi-agent research systems. They recommend starting evaluating immediately with small samples in early development because changes tend to have dramatic impacts with abundant low-hanging fruit. For scalable evaluation, they use LLM-as-judge for grading outputs against criteria like factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, and source quality. Human evaluation catches what automation misses, finding edge cases like hallucinated answers on unusual queries or subtle source selection biases. Additionally, for agents that mutate state over many turns, they focus on end-state evaluation rather than turn-by-turn analysis to ensure agents achieve the correct final state.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-agent system evaluation methodology?
choices: Start evaluating immediately with small samples
Apply human evaluation for edge cases

questions.lessonContent: Research outputs are difficult to evaluate programmatically since they are free-form text and rarely have a single correct answer. Anthropic used an LLM judge that evaluated each output against specific criteria in a rubric: factual accuracy (whether claims match sources), citation accuracy (whether cited sources match the claims), completeness (whether all requested aspects are covered), source quality (whether it used primary sources over lower-quality secondary sources), and tool efficiency (whether it used the right tools a reasonable number of times). They experimented with multiple judges but found that a single LLM call with one prompt outputting scores from 0.0-1.0 and a pass-fail grade was most consistent and aligned with human judgments.
questions.question: According to the source content, how many criteria does the LLM-as-judge evaluation use?

questions.lessonContent: Multi-agent systems consume significantly more tokens than single-agent chat interactions. In Anthropic's data, agents typically use about 4× more tokens than chat interactions, while multi-agent systems use about 15× more tokens than chats. This high token consumption means multi-agent systems require tasks where the value is high enough to pay for the increased performance.
questions.question: Multi-agent systems use less tokens than single-agent chat interactions.

questions.lessonContent: Production agents often engage in conversations spanning hundreds of turns, requiring careful context management strategies. As conversations extend, standard context windows become insufficient, necessitating intelligent compression and memory mechanisms. Anthropic implemented patterns where agents summarize completed work phases and store essential information in external memory before proceeding to new tasks. When context limits approach, agents can spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts while maintaining continuity through careful handoffs. They can retrieve stored context like the research plan from their memory rather than losing previous work when reaching the context limit.
questions.question: Which of the following describes Anthropic's approach to handling context limits in long-horizon conversations?
choices: Agents compress all previous context into a single summary without external storage
Agents use synchronous execution to manage context across all subagents
Agents simply restart from the beginning when context limits are reached
Agents summarize completed work and store it in external memory, then spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts when limits approach
questions.explanation: The correct approach is that agents summarize completed work phases and store essential information in external memory before proceeding to new tasks. When context limits approach, they spawn fresh subagents with clean contexts while maintaining continuity through careful handoffs and retrieving stored context.

questions.lessonContent: Anthropic's evaluation methodology follows a progressive scaling approach. First, they recommend starting with small samples in early agent development, as changes tend to have dramatic impacts and effect sizes are large enough to spot with just a few test cases. Second, they scale the evaluation process using an LLM judge that can evaluate hundreds of outputs against criteria like factual accuracy and completeness. Third, they add human evaluation to catch edge cases that automation misses, such as hallucinated answers on unusual queries or subtle source selection biases.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the multi-agent system evaluation process?

questions.lessonContent: Text embeddings provide a mathematical measure of the similarity or relatedness between given text queries. This numerical representation allows computers to understand semantic relationships between pieces of text. Embeddings are fundamental to various natural language processing applications because they convert textual information into dense vector representations that capture meaning. The technology enables machines to perform tasks like finding documents that are conceptually related even when they do not share exact wording.
questions.question: What do text embeddings provide a measure of?

questions.lessonTitle: Base Model Selection for Continued Pretraining
questions.lessonContent: Before training Composer 2, the team evaluated several potential open-source base models including GLM-5, Kimi K2.5, and DeepSeek V3.2. They used three internal benchmarks to assess candidate models: FreshBench measures coding knowledge through question-answer pairs created from traces where the model had to read library source code or perform web searches; State Tracking measures the model's ability to understand past file edits using an internal benchmark similar to LoCoDiff; Codebase Perplexity measures the model's coding intelligence by computing negative log-likelihoods over their private monorepo. After evaluating these models, they selected Kimi K2.5 as the base model due to its general strong performance across all three benchmarks and additional considerations such as efficiency in their infrastructure. Kimi K2.5 is a 1.04T parameter Mixture-of-Experts model with 32B active parameters.
questions.question: What is the name of the base model selected for Composer 2 continued pretraining?

questions.lessonContent: The continued pretraining stage for Composer 2 is divided into three distinct phases. The first and most computationally intensive phase uses a 32k token sequence length where the bulk of compute is spent. The second phase is a shorter long-context extension that extends the sequence length to 256k tokens. The third and final phase is a short Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) phase focused on targeted coding tasks. During training, the team measured evaluation loss on their internal codebase and observed that the loss decreases log-linearly over the course of the training run. This three-phase approach allows the model to first build strong coding knowledge at standard context, then extend to longer contexts, and finally specialize on specific coding tasks.
questions.question: The three phases of continued pretraining are: (1) bulk compute at 32k token sequence length, (2) long-context extension to 256k tokens, and (3) short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks.

questions.lessonContent: Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layers are trained to serve the Composer 2 model faster in production through speculative decoding. These MTP layers are initialized from scratch and trained on the same data mix as the main model. To speed up convergence, the MTP layers are trained with self-distillation, which teaches the model to predict the exact logit distribution of the main LM head at each position. The MTP layers are trained atop a checkpoint cut from the middle of the continued pretraining run, not from the final checkpoint. During the final two phases of continued pretraining (the long-context extension and SFT phases), the MTP layers are included and trained jointly with the rest of the model, allowing them to benefit from the same training signal.
questions.question: How are the Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layers trained to speed up convergence?
choices: They are trained with self-distillation to predict the exact logit distribution of the main LM head at each position
They are initialized from the final checkpoint of continued pretraining for maximum performance
They are copied directly from the base model's pre-trained weights
They are trained using reinforcement learning with reward signals
questions.explanation: The correct answer is self-distillation because the content explicitly states: 'To speed up convergence, we train the MTP layers with self-distillation, teaching the model to predict the exact logit distribution of the main LM head at each position.' The other options are incorrect: MTP layers are initialized from scratch (not copied), they are trained on a middle checkpoint (not final), and they are trained during continued pretraining (not with RL).

questions.lessonTitle: Module 1: Foundations and Continued Pretraining - Ordering Question
questions.lessonContent: In the Composer 2 continued pretraining process, the model first selects a base model (Kimi K2.5) as the foundation. Then, the continued pretraining phase conducts the bulk of training at 32k token sequence length. Following this, a long-context extension phase expands the sequence length to 256k tokens. Finally, a short SFT phase on targeted coding tasks completes the specialization. The Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) layers are trained during the final two phases (long-context and SFT).
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 continued pretraining pipeline?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonTitle: KL Divergence Estimator in Composer 2 RL Training
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence for regularization in reinforcement learning training. Many open-source implementations of RL estimate KL with the estimator k3 = (r - 1) - log r, which is defined in Schulman and is an unbiased estimator that reduces variance when p and q are close. However, research has shown that the variance of k3 increases drastically as p and q diverge, which is problematic for large KL values. Therefore, Composer 2 uses the standard estimator k1 = -log r instead, which avoids the variance blow-up issue even though it may introduce some bias.
questions.question: What KL divergence estimator does Composer 2 use in its RL training?

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses a self-summarization technique introduced in Composer 1.5 to enable the model to work across long horizons. Each training rollout can involve multiple generations chained together by summaries, rather than being limited to a single prompt-response pair. The final reward is used for all tokens produced by the model in the chain, which upweights both successful agent responses and the self-summarizations that made them work. At the same time, poor summaries that lose critical information are downweighted. As Composer trains, it learns to use self-summaries to process more information even with a limited context window, and for hard examples it often self-summarizes multiple times.
questions.question: In self-summarization, the final reward is applied to all tokens produced by the model in the chain.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonTitle: Length Penalty Formula in Composer 2 RL Training
questions.lessonContent: To incentivize the model to produce solutions quickly on easy requests while allowing it to think longer on hard requests, Composer 2 adds a concave down and increasing nonlinear length penalty to the reward. The formula is Clength{k,q}(x) = ((1 + kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1 - q)), where k and q are hyperparameters that define the curvature of the penalty. The input x is a weighted combination of thinking tokens, tool calling tokens, tool output tokens, final message tokens, number of tool calls, and number of turns of a rollout. The nonlinearity reflects that on easy tasks, achievable with only a few tool calls, every additional bit of effort is felt more acutely than in long-horizon tasks where the agent might iterate for hundreds of tool calls.
questions.question: Which formula represents the nonlinear length penalty used in Composer 2 to incentivize efficient agent behavior?
questions.explanation: The correct formula is Clength{k,q}(x) = ((1 + kx)^(1-q) - 1) / (k(1 - q)), which creates a concave down, increasing penalty that pushes the model to be quick on easy tasks while allowing more thinking on harder tasks.

questions.moduleTitle: Module 2: Reinforcement Learning and Agent Behavior
questions.lessonContent: In the Composer 2 reinforcement learning pipeline, the training process follows a specific sequence. First, a problem is sampled from the training distribution. Then, multiple rollouts are simulated from the agent with different solution approaches. After rollouts are generated, auxiliary rewards are applied to shape desired behaviors such as coding style and communication quality. Additionally, a nonlinear length penalty is applied to incentivize the model to produce quick solutions on easy tasks while allowing more thinking time on complex problems. Finally, the model weights are updated based on the computed advantages from the rollouts. This process iterates to progressively improve agent behavior.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the Composer 2 reinforcement learning training pipeline?

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench is an internal evaluation suite comprising tasks drawn from actual coding sessions of the Cursor engineering team. The benchmark tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications than public benchmarks, with a median of 181 lines changed compared to just 7-10 lines for SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual. Additionally, CursorBench prompts are more under-specified, featuring a median description length of only 390 characters versus 1,185-3,055 characters for public benchmarks. This combination of broad execution scope and high intent ambiguity reflects the difficulty of real-world software engineering. The benchmark is continually updated as user workflows evolve and agent capabilities improve.
questions.question: What is the median number of lines changed in CursorBench tasks compared to SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual?

questions.lessonContent: CursorBench evaluation tasks require substantially more extensive code modifications than public benchmarks. Specifically, the median number of lines changed in CursorBench is 181, while SWE-bench Verified and Multilingual tasks typically require only 7-10 lines changed. questions.lessonContent: Composer 2 uses different parallelism configurations for continued pretraining and reinforcement learning phases. During continued pretraining, the system employs Expert Parallelism (EP) with 8 experts and Context Parallelism (CP) with 2 ranks (EP=8, CP=2). For the reinforcement learning phase, the configuration changes to EP=8, CP=8. The infrastructure also includes a global sequence packing stage before each training step to ensure balanced Data Parallel (DP) compute load, particularly important because different rollouts can result in very different sequence lengths.
questions.question: What parallelism configuration does Composer 2 use for continued pretraining and RL training phases?
choices: EP=8, CP=2 for continued pretraining; EP=8, CP=8 for RL
EP=8, CP=4 for continued pretraining; EP=8, CP=4 for RL
EP=4, CP=4 for continued pretraining; EP=8, CP=4 for RL
EP=16, CP=2 for continued pretraining; EP=16, CP=8 for RL
questions.explanation: The correct configuration is EP=8, CP=2 for continued pretraining and EP=8, CP=8 for RL, as explicitly stated in the infrastructure section of the technical report.

questions.lessonContent: The evaluation workflow in Composer 2 follows a systematic approach to assess model performance on real-world coding tasks. First, for each task in CursorBench, we initialize the codebase environment - this creates the same development environment that the agent will operate in. Second, we initialize the task prompt, which provides the agent with its specific coding task or bug fix request. Third, we run the agent exactly as it would execute in our production environment, allowing it to interact with the codebase, make edits, run commands, and attempt to solve the task. After the agent completes its work, we then compute accuracy metrics to determine task success and measure efficiency metrics such as completion tokens, latency, and inference cost.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in the CursorBench evaluation pipeline?

questions.lessonTitle: Managing Allowed Tools in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: By default, Claude Code requests permission for any action that might modify your system, including file writes, many bash commands, and MCP tools. This deliberately conservative approach prioritizes safety. There are four ways to manage allowed tools: Select 'Always allow' when prompted during a session, use the /permissions command after starting Claude Code to add or remove tools from the allowlist, manually edit your .claude/settings.json or ~/.claude.json (the former is recommended for team sharing), or use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions.
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a method for managing allowed tools in Claude Code?
choices: Select 'Always allow' when prompted during a session
Use the /config command to set tool permissions
Use the --allowedTools CLI flag for session-specific permissions
Use the /permissions command to add or remove tools
questions.explanation: The correct method is using the /permissions command, not /config. The four documented methods are: selecting 'Always allow' when prompted, using /permissions command, manually editing settings files, and using the --allowedTools CLI flag.

questions.moduleTitle: Setting Up and Customizing Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: When customizing your Claude Code setup, you begin by creating a CLAUDE.md file that Claude automatically pulls into context when starting a conversation. Once you've created your CLAUDE.md files, you should then tune them like any frequently used prompt, refining the content through experimentation to determine what produces the best instruction following from the model. Finally, after establishing and tuning your CLAUDE.md files, you can curate Claude's list of allowed tools to permit additional tools that you know are safe for your workflow.
questions.question: What is the correct order of steps in customizing your Claude Code setup?

questions.moduleTitle: Extending Claude with Tools and Workflows
questions.lessonTitle: MCP Configuration Methods in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code functions as both an MCP server and client, allowing it to connect to any number of MCP servers to access their tools. MCP tools can be configured in three distinct ways to control their availability across different contexts. First, in project config which makes tools available only when running Claude Code in that specific directory. Second, in global config which makes tools available in all projects. Third, in a checked-in .mcp.json file which makes tools available to anyone working in your codebase, such as adding Puppeteer and Sentry servers so every engineer can use them out of the box. When troubleshooting MCP configuration issues, launching Claude with the --mcp-debug flag helps identify problems.
questions.question: In how many different ways can MCP tools be configured in Claude Code?

questions.moduleTitle: Extending Claude with Tools and Workflows
questions.lessonContent: For repeated workflows like debugging loops or log analysis, you can store prompt templates in Markdown files within the .claude/commands folder. These become available through the slash commands menu when you type /. Custom slash commands can include the special keyword $ARGUMENTS to pass parameters from command invocation. For example, creating a file called fix-github-issue.md with content including 'Please analyze and fix the GitHub issue: $ARGUMENTS' would allow you to use /project:fix-github-issue 1234 to fix issue #1234.
questions.question: Custom slash commands support the $ARGUMENTS keyword to pass parameters from command invocation.

questions.moduleTitle: Extending Claude with Tools and Workflows
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. To enable headless mode, you use the -p flag with a prompt. For streaming JSON output, the --output-format stream-json flag is used. However, headless mode does not persist between sessions, meaning you must trigger it each session. A practical example of headless mode is using it for issue triage, where Claude inspects new issues as they come in and assigns appropriate labels.
questions.question: Which combination of CLI flags is used to enable headless mode with streaming JSON output in Claude Code?
questions.explanation: The correct answer is -p with --output-format stream-json. The content explicitly states to use the -p flag with a prompt to enable headless mode, and --output-format stream-json for streaming JSON output.

questions.lessonTitle: Enabling Headless Mode in Claude Code
questions.lessonContent: Claude Code includes headless mode for non-interactive contexts like CI, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and automation. To enable headless mode, you use the -p flag along with your prompt. The --output-format stream-json flag can be used for streaming JSON output. This mode allows Claude to run without user interaction, making it suitable for automated workflows and scripts.
questions.question: What is the CLI flag used to enable headless mode in Claude Code?

questions.lessonContent: Headless mode in Claude Code is designed for non-interactive contexts such as CI pipelines, pre-commit hooks, build scripts, and various automation tasks. When you trigger headless mode with the appropriate flags, it executes your prompt and returns results without requiring user interaction. However, once the session completes, the headless mode does not persist—you must trigger it again each time you want to run Claude in headless mode.
questions.question: Headless mode in Claude Code persists between sessions, allowing you to continue where you left off.

questions.lessonContent: When working on multiple independent tasks with Claude Code, git worktrees provide a lightweight solution for running multiple Claude sessions simultaneously. Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, with each worktree having its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog. This enables you to have one Claude refactoring your authentication system while another builds a data visualization component, with each working at full speed without merge conflicts. To use this approach, you create worktrees with git worktree add ../project-feature-a feature-a, then launch Claude in each worktree with cd ../project-feature-a && claude.
questions.question: Which approach allows you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, enabling multiple Claude sessions to work simultaneously on independent tasks?
choices: Multiple git checkouts in separate folders
questions.explanation: Git worktrees allow you to check out multiple branches from the same repository into separate directories, with each worktree having its own working directory with isolated files while sharing the same Git history and reflog, enabling multiple Claude sessions to work simultaneously on different independent tasks.

questions.lessonContent: In the multi-Claude verification workflow described in the documentation, the process involves having one Claude write code while another reviews it. First, you use Claude to write code. Then, you run /clear or start a second Claude in another terminal. Next, the second Claude reviews the first Claude's work. After that, you start another Claude to read both the code and review feedback. Finally, this Claude edits the code based on the feedback. This separation of writing and reviewing often yields better results than having a single Claude handle everything.
